لما أبني AI Agent بيرد على استفسارات الطلبات فيه سؤال لازم أجاوب عليه قبل ما أخليه يرد على العميل

هو عرف منين إن ده الطلب اللي العميل بيسأل عنه
خلينا نقول إن عميل بعت على WhatsApp وقال فين طلبي

العميل عنده طلبين لسه مفتوحين ومبعتش رقم الطلب
الـ Agent ممكن يفهم السؤال كويس جدًا وبرضه يختار الطلب الغلط

وساعتها هيبعت للعميل حالة شحنة فعلية من السيستم بس الشحنة دي مش بتاعته

وده بالنسبالي أخطر من إنه يرد بإجابة مش عارفها
لأن العميل مش هيعرف إن الـ Agent خمّن هو هيعتبر إن المعلومة دي جاية من السيستم فعلًا

عشان كده لو الـ Agent مش قادر يحدد الطلب المفروض يسأل العميل عن رقم الطلب أو معلومة تساعده يوصله للطلب الصح

وبعد ما يحدد الطلب لازم يتأكد إن الطلب ده يخص العميل قبل ما يعرض أي تفاصيل

ولو لسه فيه شك الأفضل يحوّل المحادثة لموظف بدل ما يكمّل على أساس تخمين

وده بيفرق معايا في طريقة تصميم الـ AI Agent

مش كفاية إنه يفهم السؤال لازم كمان يكون فيه قواعد واضحة تحدد إمتى يقدر يختار وإمتى لازم يسأل وإمتى يوقف ويطلب تدخل بشري

لأن في الآخر مش المهم إن الـ Agent يرد بسرعة

المهم إنه يرد على العميل بالمعلومة الصح




When building an AI Agent to handle order inquiries, there's one question I need to answer before letting it respond to customers

How does it know which order the customer is actually asking about

Let's say a customer sends a WhatsApp message asking where their order is

They have two open orders and haven't provided an order number

The Agent might understand the question perfectly and still pick the wrong order

It could end up sharing real tracking information from the system, but for a shipment that doesn't belong to that customer

And to me, that's more concerning than the Agent simply not knowing the answer

The customer has no way of knowing the Agent made a guess. They'll assume the information came directly from the system

That's why, if the Agent can't identify the right order, it should ask for the order number or another detail that helps narrow it down

Once it finds the order, it also needs to verify that it actually belongs to the customer before sharing any details

And if there's still uncertainty, it's better to hand the conversation over to a human than keep guessing

This is something I think about when designing AI Agents

Understanding the question isn't enough. There also need to be clear rules for when the Agent can make a decision, when it should ask for more information, and when it needs to stop and involve a human

Because in the end, a fast response isn't what matters most

Getting the right information to the right customer does

We built a WhatsApp Business agent workspace on Laravel + Filament.
Three lessons you won’t find in the docs:
1. Let the 24-hour window drive the UI. Inside it you can reply with free text; after it, only approved templates. If the window closes mid-reply, the draft survives. AI reads the conversation and picks the template, filling the variables from context. A human always presses send.
2. Telegram beats a separate app for your team. One group, a topic per customer with Take / Transfer / Close buttons. Agents reply from their phone, where they already are.
3. Opt-in is required for any first message, even a service one. Our costliest bug: our own “Annulla” (cancel) button unsubscribed customers forever. Your do-not-contact list must survive both customer data erasure and key rotation.

A week must have felt like a lifetime for the two Ukrainian women who escaped from occupied Oleshky, now known globally as the town where Russian soldiers are using civilians as a human shield.

People are doing good work here and we should back them.

elements.content:
"AI hacked a government in two hours." On Sunday night, part of that story was retracted.

On Friday, Unit 42 said an agentic AI attacker broke into a European government agency through the PHP2Shell flaws.

Within two hours, it reportedly had password hashes and MFA secrets. Then it went after Domain Admin.

On Sunday evening, the team retracted the update. It can't confirm the way in was PHP2Shell.

The "AI tell" was always thin. It was command output wrapped in tidy markers like ==PASSWD==. Humans and pentest tools do that too.

But here's the part that got skipped. Read the steps again, with the AI taken out:

🔐 MFA secrets an attacker on the web tier could read
🗝️ Database credentials sitting on an internet-facing host
🌐 A web server that could talk to the domain controller
👤 Anonymous LDAP queries against the DC
🔁 NTLM relay still working
👑 A short path towards Domain Admin

Every one of those is an old, known gap. None needs a frontier model. None is fixed by better alignment.

Each one is fixed by a boundary most teams could name in their sleep.

The same week:

🧪 CrowdStrike saw only probing and failed PHP2Shell attempts
🧯 A lab security lead told CISOs to go to their boards "for the basics"
🤖 Even the Georgia "Claude got the vote counts" story turned out to be a token handed to anyone, plus agent egress nobody was watching

Whether the keyboard belonged to a model or a person is the least useful fact for defenders. The steps are the useful part.

I wrote up what was claimed, what was withdrawn, and the checks I'd run this week.

Full article below 👇

When a report says "AI attacker", does it change what your team does on Monday, or just how the story gets told to the board?

Space, Telecom & AI - A New Era of Connectivity !

I’ve been closely following SpaceX’s recent announcements and what they could mean for the future of telecom. One thing is becoming increasingly clear: the boundaries of the telco industry are changing.

As space companies move deeper into mobile connectivity, the traditional distinction between satellite and terrestrial networks will continue to blur. This is more than a coverage story; it could reshape how networks are built, how services are delivered, and where value is created.

For telcos, the opportunity is to look beyond the competitive threat and rethink their role in this evolving ecosystem. Combining terrestrial networks with satellite connectivity, cloud, edge computing, and AI could unlock new business models, enable intelligent network operations, and extend digital services to places and industries that remain underserved.

The strategic question is not simply how telcos respond to SpaceX, but how they position themselves to lead in a world where connectivity is increasingly ubiquitous and AI drives differentiation.

The next evolution of telecom will be about more than connecting people and places. It will be about connecting networks, compute, and intelligence across the ground, the sky, and the cloud.

A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, a week after it was announced by US First Lady, Melania Trump.

The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.

Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.

Oleshky is on the south bank of the river Dnipro, which forms the front line in the Kherson region. The remaining residents have been desperately short of food and other essential supplies.

Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.

“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.

Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.

The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children:

elements.content:
My main Telegram bot is where I read news cards with approve/reject buttons and watch voice-blog previews. But it was also the inbox for every infrastructure alarm on vitalii.no — token warnings, feature-discovery reports, rewrite-stats summaries, digest-watchdog pings. On a bad day three or four of those landed at once and buried the actual content I was supposed to act on.

So I split the two jobs apart. Six different places that used to send into my main bot now check for a separate technical-alarms bot first, and only fall back to the old channel if that separate bot isn't configured.

The six are a mix of Supabase Edge Functions and shell scripts, and each one reads the new technical bot's token and chat ID the same way, so the fallback behaves identically no matter which one fires.

The content channel is just content again. Six kinds of technical noise moved out on their own, and if I ever forget to set the new credentials somewhere, that one spot just falls back to the old bot exactly like before — nothing silently stops arriving.

AI Telco Shorts Episode #2 | Perspectives from Asia with Dr. Rainer Deutschmann, Chief Strategy & Transformation Officer, Axiata Group.

My key takeaway: Telcos are the ultimate AI laboratories, sitting on billions of real-world transactions, customer interactions, and network events that generate insights no one else can replicate.

AI is compounding at an extraordinary rate, with hardware capability, AI investment and algorithmic breakthroughs...all growing exponentially.

So what should telcos do now?

1️⃣ Define 'where you play'
Everyone can buy a model. Focus on what you have earned, not what anyone can buy. Telcos' competitive advantage lies in their data, customer relationships, trust, and ability to learn faster than the competition.

2️⃣ Redefine 'how you run'
Build a self-learning organisation. Simplify before you automate, automate before you agentify, and embed AI into the fabric of business processes.

3️⃣ Decide 'where humans sit'
As AI takes on more tasks, the role of humans increasingly becomes that of directors, evaluators, and boundary-setters...steering the organisation, judging outcomes, and intervening when exceptions demand it.

Watch episode two and share your perspective: which of these actions are most urgent for telcos today, and where is the industry still falling behind?

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜-𝗥𝗔𝗡 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 𝗶𝘁.

I’m encouraged by the engineering progress. I’m less convinced by the assumption that putting AI compute into a network automatically creates a business.

This week’s T-Mobile AI-RAN call and Elisa’s trial combining radio and AI workloads move technical feasibility forward. AT&T’s separate AI networking MVP explores another part of the problem: controlling how applications reach models, handle data and consume budget.

There is a bigger telecom story here. The location of computing is becoming part of the service decision.

An industrial application may need inference near a machine. A consumer assistant may keep sensitive processing on the device. Other workloads will run more economically in a central cloud. The operator’s opportunity is to make those choices work together without asking customers to manage the boundaries.

That could change what telcos sell, how they design networks and how they support customers. But first, we need to separate two investment cases: AI that improves radio performance, and AI applications that share network computing resources. 𝗔 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿.

Shared infrastructure introduces a practical tension. Radio processing has deadlines; AI demand can be unpredictable. Protecting connectivity may leave compute idle. Selling that capacity too aggressively could compromise the service customers already pay for.

The commercial design therefore belongs in the architecture discussion. What capacity can be committed? Who pays for reservations? Can the application move elsewhere? Does the price cover power, software, support and partner margins?

I would insist on those answers before approving a wider rollout.

Over time, I see a credible role for telcos in operating distributed AI services. Their reach matters, but the advantage must be earned through reliable delivery, customer access and disciplined economics. Hyperscalers and application providers will remain formidable partners and competitors.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁?

HCLTech’s network engineering, AI infrastructure and managed operations capabilities are relevant here: helping operators test the architecture and operating model together before committing at scale.

🚀 Big news in the realm of cybersecurity! 

Russia's government is considering blocking access to the Tor network and similar privacy tools in response to an anti-child-abuse campaign. This move raises critical questions about privacy, security, and the ongoing tug-of-war between safeguarding citizens and protecting online anonymity. 

Here’s what we see unfolding:

- **Privacy under fire:** Just like the early 2000s when governments first started cracking down on encryption technologies, we’re witnessing another chapter in the battle for online privacy. The implications? A potential chilling effect on whistleblowers, activists, and anyone seeking to protect their online identity.

- **Tech industry shake-up:** As more countries look to take control of digital spaces, we may see a rise in decentralized networks and privacy-focused innovations. Developers might pivot to create stronger, more resilient tools that prioritize user anonymity without compromising safety. 

- **Future impact:** If Russia pushes this agenda, expect a ripple effect. Other nations might follow suit, leading to a fragmented internet where access to privacy tools varies widely. A digital Iron Curtain, anyone? 

As IT professionals and cybersecurity experts, it’s our job to stay ahead of these trends and advocate for balanced solutions that protect both privacy and safety. The tech landscape is evolving rapidly, and it’s crucial we engage in these conversations.

elements.content:
1956: the shipping container changed global trade.
2027 may be the year telecom starts doing something similar with the network.

In October 2026, BICS and Proximus Global pushed several signals in the same direction: Network APIs, 5G Standalone services and more programmable, secure enterprise connectivity.

The common thread is simple: standardisation.

The container did not create global trade.
It made movement easier, repeatable and scalable.

Network APIs could do the same for telecom by turning capabilities such as identity, authentication, location and quality on demand into services enterprises can consume directly.

That could make 2027 a real inflection point for telco B2B.

The next growth engine may not come from selling more connectivity, but from making the network easier to integrate, automate and monetize inside enterprise workflows.

Source: BICS / Proximus Global, October 2026 announcements.
